AMBIGUITY_RULES.rule_text: Retain a candidate when the mention is the complement of the main predicate, even if the sentence begins with a contrastive opener, contains a parenthetical with coordinated-clause alternatives, or ends with a purpose qualifier-clause. Contrastive discourse markers and parenthetical alternatives should not demote a mention that remains attached to the main assertion. Reject cases where only the coordinated alternatives are present and no element mention appears as the complement of the main predicate.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.example_block:
TP: "By contrast, all entries remain in the second element (for example, under one option or another option) to keep the first element separate from the summary." 
FP: "By contrast, all entries remain under one option or another option to keep the first element separate from the summary."
AMBIGUITY_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule uses only sentence-level attachment: main predicate complement versus parenthetical alternatives and trailing qualifier-clause material. These are general discourse cues that recur regardless of decomposition style or naming scheme.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: contrastive opener, parenthetical coordinated-clause, and purpose qualifier-clause can occur in any documentation style, but the complement of the main predicate remains the same syntactic anchor. The rule preserves that anchor without relying on style-specific semantics. Passes.

AMBIGUITY_RULES.rule_text: Permit multiple approvals from one sentence when distinct exact-match mentions occur in different syntactic functions, such as one in the main predicate and another in a qualifier-clause or coordinated-clause. A contrastive opener or coordinated-clause boundary should not suppress approval by itself if each approved mention has its own local predicate attachment. Reject only when a candidate lacks local syntactic support and is present only by topic carryover.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.example_block:
TP: "However, the record is written to [X] to isolate [Y] from direct updates." -> link to [X] and link to [Y]
FP: "However, the record is written externally to isolate later processing from direct updates." -> no link
AMBIGUITY_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule is about clause structure, not architecture semantics. Main-predicate mentions and qualifier-clause mentions can co-occur in any documentation style, and contrast markers are discourse devices rather than style indicators.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five can express two exact-match mentions in one sentence with one attached to the main predicate and another attached to a purpose or qualifier-clause. The rule does not assume any specific component type or interaction mechanism; it only preserves approvals when separate exact-match mentions have separate syntactic anchors. Passes.

AMBIGUITY_RULES.rule_text: Retain a candidate when it is the complement of the main predicate, even if the sentence begins with a contrastive opener, contains a parenthetical with coordinated-clause alternatives, or ends with a qualifier-clause. Contrast markers and parenthetical alternatives should lower confidence only for the alternative phrases themselves, not for the explicit mention anchored to the main assertion. Reject cases where only generic coordinated alternatives appear and no explicit mention is licensed by the main predicate.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.example_block:
TP: "By contrast, all items remain in the archive element (either in a primary location or a secondary location) to keep the index separate." -> retain the archive element.
FP: "By contrast, all items remain in a primary location or a secondary location to keep the index separate." -> do not approve a link because no explicit element mention is anchored.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule uses discourse markers, parenthetical structure, coordinated-clause handling, and complement status under the main predicate. These are general sentence-structure cues that apply independently of implementation style or domain terminology.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: each style can be described with contrastive openers, parenthetical alternatives, and purpose qualifier-clauses, but the main-predicate complement remains the same structural anchor across all five. The rule neither assumes any style-specific component type nor any domain noun. Passes.

AMBIGUITY_RULES.rule_text: When a sentence contains multiple mentions, prioritize subject-position mention, apposition, and copular complement as primary candidates for linking. Treat object-position mentions inside predicate phrases or qualifier-clauses as contextual unless they receive independent support by exact-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, or a later sentence where they move into subject-position. A relation from subject to object does not by itself transfer identity to the object mention.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.example_block:
TP: S1: The alpha unit exchanges messages with the beta unit. S2: The alpha unit also rewrites the payload.
FP: S1: The alpha unit exchanges messages with the beta unit. S2: It retries after a timeout.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is based on syntactic prominence and clause structure rather than any specific interaction mechanism. Subject-position versus object-position is a stable cue across architecture descriptions of many forms.
AMBIGUITY_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in all five, relation sentences can mention another element in object-position, but that mention is still secondary unless later promoted or independently defined. Subject prominence and qualifier-clause demotion remain valid across the five. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a subject-position or predicate-introduced multi-word-phrase is followed by a parenthetical that contains a coordinated-clause with two or more noun-phrase candidates, extract each parenthetical noun phrase as a standalone candidate. If the parenthetical is attached to a head-noun denoting a location-like or container-like mention in the same clause, treat each extracted noun phrase as an alias-defined-parenthetically or sub-element candidate of that introduced phrase. Do not extract from parentheticals whose content is only explanatory modifier material and lacks noun-phrase candidates.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "A dedicated holding area (a primary segment or a secondary segment) is referenced in the follow-up-sentence." -> extract separate candidates for "primary segment" and "secondary segment".
FP: "A dedicated holding area (for clarity and consistency) is referenced in the follow-up-sentence." -> do not extract standalone candidates from the parenthetical.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on parenthetical structure, coordinated-clause form, and noun-phrase extraction, not on any domain lexicon or component naming convention. It generalizes wherever documentation introduces one phrase and then refines it through parenthetical alternatives.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, parenthetical coordinated noun phrases can function as alias-defined-parenthetically or sub-element evidence independent of architecture-specific vocabulary. The trigger is purely syntactic: parenthetical attachment plus coordinated noun phrases after an introduced head-noun. No style-specific assumptions are required. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a sentence has a clear subject-position mention and the main predicate introduces a second mention in object position or in a destination phrase, extract both mentions as separate candidates. Do not require the second mention to be the head-noun of the sentence; predicate-governed object and destination mentions are eligible when they are part of the main assertion. Do not promote mentions that appear only in a temporal modifier, condition, or other non-argument qualifier-clause.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The first element forwards a message to the second element and records the outcome." 
FP: "The first element forwards a message after the second element becomes available."
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule depends only on predicate structure, argument position, and distinction between main assertion versus modifier material. Those cues are discourse-syntactic and do not rely on any domain noun, role noun, or implementation convention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, subject-position plus main-predicate object or destination phrase remains a stable syntactic signal, while temporal or conditional modifier mentions remain non-arguments. The rule does not depend on any style-specific naming or topology, only on argument structure. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a predicate states that an artifact is kept, written, placed, or maintained in a location-denoting multi-word-phrase, do not require the target mention to be the head-noun of that location phrase. If the same sentence contains a qualifier-clause, modifier, namespace-prefix, or alias-defined-parenthetically mention that partially matches the target and signals a container-of or ownership relation rather than mere adjacency, allow extraction to the qualified mention. Reject when the added phrase is only locative, comparative, or incidental and does not re-specify what the location belongs to.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "Each entry is written to a separate location associated with the audit namespace-prefix." -> link to the partially matched qualified mention because the predicate plus qualifier indicates the container-of relation.
FP: "Each entry is written to a separate location near the audit namespace-prefix." -> do not link because the added phrase is only locative adjacency.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on predicate structure, qualifier-clause behavior, and partial-match or namespace-prefix cues. It does not assume any role noun, domain noun, or style-specific mechanism; it generalizes wherever documentation names a location phrase while the intended target appears in a dependent phrase.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can express storage or placement with a location head-noun while the intended referent appears in a qualifier-clause, modifier, alias-defined-parenthetically form, or namespace-prefix. The acceptance condition is syntactic-semantic and the rejection condition blocks mere adjacency, so the rule is not tied to any one architecture style. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: Approve extraction when one exact-match mention appears in subject-position and a second exact-match mention appears later in the predicate as object, prepositional complement, or qualifier-clause target. Do not require a copular form, apposition, or introducing-sentence pattern if the predicate explicitly directs an action toward the later mention. A definite-article, head-noun, or namespace-prefix modifier around the later mention may strengthen the extraction but is not required.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "When processing begins, [X] forwards the update to the [Y] module." -> link to [Y]
FP: "When processing begins, [X] forwards the update for later handling." -> no link
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on sentence-position and predicate structure: subject-position source plus later exact-match target in the predicate. That discourse configuration is independent of implementation vocabulary and remains valid wherever documentation describes one mention acting toward another mention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can place one exact-match mention in subject-position and another exact-match mention in object or qualifier-clause position under a transitive predicate. The rule does not rely on any role noun, storage wording, or style-specific topology; it only uses syntactic placement and exact-match presence. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a head-noun phrase in object-position or qualifier-clause is immediately followed by a parenthetical containing coordinated-clause noun phrases, extract each parenthetical noun phrase as a standalone candidate if the main predicate assigns placement, containment, or location to the outer phrase. Treat each extracted parenthetical noun phrase as linked by alias-defined-parenthetically or sub-element-of to the outer phrase, and preserve both exact-match and partial-match forms. Do not extract from a parenthetical whose content lacks noun-phrase structure or functions only as adverbial explanation.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The items are placed in a reserved area (a remote unit and a local unit) before later processing." -> extract separate candidates for both parenthetical noun phrases.
FP: "The items are placed in a reserved area (for stability and for speed) before later processing." -> do not extract candidates from the parenthetical.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on parenthetical structure, coordinated noun-phrase form, and predicate scope. It does not rely on any domain lexicon or architecture-specific naming convention, so it applies wherever documentation introduces an outer phrase and then enumerates internal alternatives or aliases in parentheses.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can use the same parenthetical coordinated noun-phrase pattern after a location or containment predicate, independent of component type. The trigger is syntactic: head-noun + parenthetical + coordinated noun phrases under one predicate. No style-specific role noun is required. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a multi-word-phrase or exact-match mention appears in subject-position and is immediately followed by a copular predicate, apposition, or clear relational predicate, treat that sentence as positive structural evidence for the subject mention. Accept forms where the predicate assigns identity, responsibility, containment, or cross-reference, even if the mention is not repeated elsewhere in the local window. Do not promote a generic head-noun phrase that appears only in predicate position without a subject-position antecedent.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The North Unit is the primary coordination point."
FP: "The primary coordination point is described below."
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on sentence-position, predicate form, and antecedent anchoring. It does not rely on any domain lexicon or style-specific naming convention, so it applies wherever documentation uses definitional or relational sentences.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can introduce an element by placing the mention in subject-position and assigning a predicate with identity or relation information. The cue is syntactic and discourse-based rather than architectural. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.rule_text: When a sentence contains an explicit mention in subject-position and the main predicate introduces a second explicit mention in object position or in a destination phrase, extract both mentions as separate candidates. Do not require the second mention to be the head-noun of the sentence if it is structurally licensed by the predicate. Do not promote mentions that appear only in a temporal, causal, or other modifier-clause not selected by the main predicate.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The first element forwards a message to the second element and records the outcome." -> extract the first element and the second element.
FP: "The first element forwards a message after the second element starts." -> do not extract the second element from the modifier-clause as a destination target.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on predicate-argument structure, sentence-position, and modifier versus complement status. Those cues are discourse-syntactic and do not depend on any particular architecture vocabulary or naming convention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_EXTRACTION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can express one explicit mention as subject-position and another as object or destination phrase under the same predicate; the extraction cue is purely syntactic and remains valid regardless of style-specific organization. No style requires the target mention to be the head-noun, and the modifier-clause exclusion is likewise style-neutral. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: Do not down-rank an otherwise valid candidate solely because the sentence-position begins with a contrastive or discourse-marking opener. Judge mention validity from the main predicate and its local noun-phrase structure; a sentence-initial contrast marker changes discourse relation to prior context but does not cancel a candidate introduced later in the same sentence. Reject only when the clause lacks a concrete noun-phrase candidate or when the predicate is purely metadiscursive.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: "However, the aggregate record is maintained in a separate index space." -> keep the noun-phrase candidate in the predicate valid.
FP: "However, the earlier statement should be interpreted differently." -> do not approve a candidate because no concrete noun-phrase target is asserted.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule is about discourse markers versus clause-internal mention validity. Contrastive openers occur across documentation styles, and their presence should not suppress extraction when the predicate still asserts a concrete mention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles use contrastive sentence-position markers in prose, and in all five the marker is discourse-level rather than entity-negating. The rule relies only on sentence-position and predicate content, not on style-specific semantics. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: Do not down-rank a candidate solely because the sentence-position begins with a contrastive or concessive discourse marker. Judge mention validity from the main predicate and its argument structure: if the sentence still asserts placement, containment, or location for a noun phrase, preserve the candidate. Reject only when the sentence contains discourse contrast without a noun-phrase candidate governed by such a predicate.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: "However, the attachments remain in a separate area for later access." -> keep the area mention valid.
FP: "However, the earlier claim was inaccurate." -> do not approve any candidate from the discourse marker alone.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule separates discourse function from entity evidence. Contrastive openers occur across documentation styles, but they do not alter whether a later predicate introduces a valid mention; the decision remains grounded in syntax and predicate-argument structure.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all can contain sentence-initial contrast markers in explanatory prose, and in all five the marker is orthogonal to whether a later noun phrase is licensed by a placement or containment predicate. The rule uses only discourse-marker position and predicate structure, not style-specific semantics. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: Distinguish direct mention from possessive or nested mention. If the predicate is attached to a sub-phrase introduced through possessive, qualifier-clause, or another nested modifier, do not treat the larger phrase as directly supported unless the larger phrase itself is also the predicate-bearing mention. Namespace-prefix or partial-match overlap is not sufficient to upgrade a related structure into a direct mention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: The sentence states that "silver element" satisfies the predicate, and the exact-match phrase is the subject-position mention.
FP: The sentence states that "silver element's inner phrase" satisfies the predicate, and the linker approves "silver element" even though the predicate is attached to the nested phrase rather than the larger possessive phrase.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: The distinction between direct mention and nested mention is a general syntactic property. It applies whenever documentation uses possessive or embedded phrases, regardless of how the architecture is organized.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five can describe entities through larger phrases and sub-phrases, and predicate attachment can target either level. The rule depends only on possessive and nested phrase structure, not on style-specific semantics. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: When a sentence contains a clear relational predicate that cross-references a second mention, approve the target-side mention as linked evidence in addition to the subject-side mention if the target has exact-match, partial-match with unique antecedent, or alias-of support. Treat the relational predicate as bidirectional evidence only when the target is explicitly realized as a noun phrase in the same clause or coordinated-clause. Do not infer a target from a predicate that names only an activity or quality without an explicit target mention.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The Ember Unit forwards updates to the Horizon Module." 
FP: "The Ember Unit improves update handling."
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule relies on cross-reference structure between subject and object mentions, not on any particular architecture vocabulary. Explicit relational predicates are a general discourse mechanism for expressing links between documented elements.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles can express relations through subject-to-target predicates with explicit noun-phrase targets. The approval condition is syntactic explicitness plus target anchoring, which is style-invariant. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: Reject a candidate sentence when the subject-position is an indefinite or generic multi-word-phrase and the sentence is centered on predicate-level description, unless the same sentence also contains target-identifying evidence such as exact-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, apposition, possessive, namespace-prefix, or section-heading alignment. Do not treat partial-match, topical similarity, or descriptive predicate content alone as sufficient identification. Prefer sentences whose head-noun phrase identifies an element rather than only describing an approach, variant, or procedure.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The exact-match unit, alias-defined-parenthetically as the short form, emits updates." 
FP: "A configurable variant emits updates when enabled."
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule depends only on subject-position form, noun-phrase specificity, and presence of sentence-local identification cues. Those signals are discourse-level and do not rely on any particular architecture organization or domain vocabulary.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, sentences can either identify an element with exact-match/apposition/alias cues or merely describe a generic approach via predicate content. The distinction is syntactic and discourse-based, not style-specific. Passes.

DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.rule_text: Do not treat a subject-position mention as identity evidence for a target element when the predicate marks a conceptual grouping, container-of relation, broader package, or descriptive umbrella. Section-heading proximity, introducing-sentence status, and partial-match to a contained phrase are weak support only; approve only if the same sentence or an immediate follow-up-sentence explicitly ties the target by exact-match, apposition, or a sub-element-of cue. A broader alias does not license identity with each contained element.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.example_block:
TP: S1: The section-heading introduces the multi-word-phrase "gamma unit." S2: The gamma unit normalizes the incoming stream.
FP: S1: The namespace-prefix gamma is a conceptual grouping for several related parts. S2: The diagram below highlights one internal element.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.why_it_transfers: The distinction between identity and grouping is expressed through predicate form and discourse structure, not through any domain-specific terminology. Any architecture document can mention broader groupings and contained elements, so the rule generalizes across styles.
DOC_KNOWLEDGE_JUDGE_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles use grouping language and local headings, and in all five a grouping mention is not equivalent to a contained element without explicit tie-back. Predicate cues such as conceptual grouping or consists-of remain non-identifying regardless of style. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Allow one discourse unit to validate multiple targets when the sentence explicitly enumerates alternatives through a coordinated-clause or parenthetical expansion. If a main clause introduces one anchor phrase and a nearby parenthetical or coordinated structure supplies multiple noun-phrase candidates linked by exact-match, partial-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, or sub-element interpretation, approve each candidate independently rather than forcing one dominant target. Do not propagate validation when the coordinated material is adjectival or adverbial only.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The reference set is associated with a local partition (an active partition and an archival partition)." -> validate links to both noun-phrase candidates.
FP: "The reference set is associated with a local partition (carefully and consistently)." -> do not validate multiple targets because the parenthetical lacks noun-phrase candidates.
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The pattern concerns multi-target support from a single sentence, which is a general property of coordinated and parenthetical syntax. It avoids assumptions about any specific architecture vocabulary and instead uses discourse-unit structure to justify parallel validation.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in every style, a sentence can enumerate multiple noun-phrase alternatives under one anchor phrase, and validation should attach to each enumerated candidate. The mechanism is syntactic propagation from one discourse unit to multiple mentions, not style-bound semantics. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Block propagated approval into a sentence that lacks an exact-match mention of the predicted target in the current sentence. A prior antecedent, section-heading, or nearby sentence-position mention is insufficient when the current sentence contains only a generic head-noun or process predicate without a local exact-match. Allow propagation only when the current sentence contains anaphora with a clear antecedent or a partial-match that is explicitly alias-defined-parenthetically.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "[X] receives the update. It then validates the payload before forwarding." -> link may propagate to [X] through clear anaphora
FP: "[X] receives the update. The payload is then validated before forwarding." -> no propagated link to an unmatched target
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule constrains validation using local mention evidence, antecedent quality, and anaphora conditions. Those are discourse-level checks that apply regardless of how the architecture is organized.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in all five, adjacent sentences can mention a target once and then continue with either clear anaphora or generic process language. Requiring a local exact-match or explicit anaphora prevents over-propagation without depending on any style-specific noun inventory. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Allow one sentence to validate multiple links when a single predicate scopes over an outer noun phrase and a parenthetical, apposition, or coordinated-clause introduces multiple noun-phrase sub-elements attached to that same head-noun. Validate each sub-element independently if each can inherit the same predicate from the outer phrase. Do not multiply links when coordination occurs at predicate level or when the coordinated material is not a noun-phrase candidate.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The records are stored in a designated area (a primary unit or a secondary unit)." -> validate one link for each parenthetical noun phrase.
FP: "The records are stored in a designated area or removed later." -> do not validate two links because the coordination is between predicates, not noun phrases.
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is based on scope and attachment: one predicate can govern several coordinated noun phrases under a shared outer phrase. That validation logic is independent of architecture style because it relies on sentence structure rather than on any particular system vocabulary.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: each style can express alternatives or sub-elements through parenthetical or appositive coordinated noun phrases under one governing predicate. The validation criterion is purely structural—shared predicate scope over multiple noun phrases—so it remains stable across all five. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Do not approve a candidate from partial-match on a shared head-noun alone. When the document mention is a multi-word-phrase, require either exact-match or compatible modifier, possessive, or qualifier-clause support for the same phrase; if the modifier structure differs, treat the match as unsupported unless another independent cue in the same local context confirms the candidate. Predicate attachment should be checked on the full phrase, not only on the head-noun.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: The introducing-sentence names the exact-match multi-word-phrase "red unit," and the follow-up-sentence repeats "the red unit" with the same predicate.
FP: A sentence contains "blue unit" inside a qualifier-clause, and the linker approves the candidate "red unit" only because both phrases share the head-noun "unit."
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule relies only on surface form, modifier structure, and local predicate attachment. Those cues are discourse-level and do not depend on any particular architecture organization or naming convention.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, documentation can contain multi-word-phrase mentions with shared head-noun and differing modifiers, so the need to validate modifier and qualifier-clause compatibility remains the same. The rule does not assume any style-specific entity type or relation, only syntactic support. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Reject or down-rank a candidate link when the only trigger is a definite-article plus generic head-noun phrase in predicate, modifier, or object position, and there is no exact-match, namespace-prefix, apposition, alias-defined-parenthetically, or strong antecedent support. Generic descriptive phrases should not be treated as component evidence unless anchored by a nearby subject-position mention or explicit cross-reference. Prefer precision over partial-match when the phrase lacks a recoverable antecedent.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The Cedar Unit stores snapshots." 
FP: "The storage path is optimized for snapshots."
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule filters weakly anchored noun phrases using only syntactic position and discourse support. Generic definite-article phrases occur in all forms of technical prose, so the rejection criterion is broadly applicable.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: each style uses generic descriptive phrases in predicates and modifiers, and those phrases are not reliable identifiers without anchoring. The rule constrains overreach using discourse evidence only. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Require sentence-local identification evidence for every linked sentence unless the sentence is explicitly anaphoric to a previously validated antecedent. Do not validate a sentence solely because it is adjacent to, coordinated with, or in a follow-up-sentence after a validated mention. In coordinated-clause or list-like sequences, re-check each sentence for its own exact-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, apposition, possessive, namespace-prefix, or licensed anaphora.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The exact-match element accepts input. It then returns a result." 
FP: "The exact-match element accepts input. Additionally, another option is available."
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is about local validation boundaries, adjacency, and coordination, which are discourse phenomena present in any architecture document. It does not assume any specific component taxonomy or style-dependent relation.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: neighboring sentences often elaborate, contrast, or enumerate, but adjacency alone never guarantees identity of reference. Revalidation by sentence-local cues or licensed anaphora is appropriate in all five settings. Passes.

VALIDATION_RULES.rule_text: Reject propagated links for coordinated-clause lists, bare enumerations, or follow-up-sentence items under a section-heading when the item lacks an explicit antecedent, exact-match, or alias-defined-parenthetically. A possessive or definite-article phrase inside an enumeration may inherit a link only if its antecedent is uniquely resolvable in the immediately preceding discourse. Section-local coherence alone is insufficient validation.
VALIDATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: S1: The theta unit has two operating forms. S2: These forms are the local form and the remote form.
FP: S1: The section-heading is "Operational Variants." S2: These options are manual mode, scheduled mode, and fallback mode.
VALIDATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: Enumeration structure and antecedent resolution are discourse phenomena that recur in all technical writing. The rule prevents heading-based overreach without assuming any particular architecture vocabulary.
VALIDATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles use headings and lists, and in all five a generic list item should not inherit an element link without explicit antecedent support. The validation criterion is purely structural and therefore stable. Passes.

COREF_RULES.rule_text: Block propagation from a demonstrative anaphora in subject-position to the nearest antecedent mention when the predicate expresses only a generic effect, outcome, or summary and the sentence lacks exact-match, repeated head-noun, possessive, apposition, or coordinated-clause continuation support. Permit propagation only when the follow-up-sentence preserves the same referent through repeated head-noun structure or another explicit antecedent-restating cue. Treat bare demonstrative subjects with abstract predicates as discourse-summary by default, not entity coreference.
COREF_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The primary unit validates the stream. This unit then emits a checksum." -> link because the anaphora repeats the head-noun and continues the predicate chain.
FP: "The primary unit validates the stream. This improves reliability." -> do not link because the demonstrative subject introduces a generic effect rather than the same antecedent.
COREF_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is anchored in anaphora resolution constraints and predicate type, not in any component category or implementation style. Demonstrative subject-position forms can summarize prior discourse in any architecture document, so requiring repeated head-noun or equivalent support is broadly applicable.
COREF_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: each style can contain follow-up-sentence anaphora, and in each style a bare demonstrative subject may refer either to a prior mention or to an abstract result. The rule uses only discourse cues—subject-position, antecedent support, coordinated-clause continuation, possessive, apposition, exact-match—so it remains invariant across styles. Passes.

COREF_RULES.rule_text: When an introducing-sentence presents a container-of relation by enumerating multiple exact-match or partial-match sub-elements, allow the next follow-up-sentence to inherit the listed item's link if that item reappears in subject-position. Require direct lexical continuity from the list item to the follow-up subject and reject propagation when the follow-up sentence begins with a generic head-noun phrase instead of a listed antecedent.
COREF_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The Atlas group contains Lumen, Orbit, and Vale. Lumen validates incoming records." 
FP: "The Atlas group contains Lumen, Orbit, and Vale. Validation of incoming records is described next."
COREF_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is based on list structure, sentence adjacency, and antecedent reuse. Enumeration followed by focused elaboration is a general documentation pattern independent of implementation style.
COREF_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five can document a larger unit followed by listed sub-elements and then elaborate one item in the next sentence. The trigger is discourse progression from list to follow-up, not style-specific content. Passes.

COREF_RULES.rule_text: Propagate a link from a definite-anaphoric subject only when a validated antecedent exists in the immediately preceding discourse and the current sentence contains an action predicate that licenses continuation of that antecedent. If the sentence contains only an effect, consequence, or result predicate and no explicit mention, do not approve a standalone link. Anaphora without validated antecedent alignment should remain unresolved rather than inherited by default.
COREF_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The conversion element rewrites the stream. This element then emits the result." -> propagation is allowed because the antecedent is explicit and the follow-up-sentence contains an action predicate.
FP: "The conversion element rewrites the stream. This can reduce delay." -> do not approve a link from the second sentence alone.
COREF_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule is based on antecedent validation, anaphora, and predicate type in follow-up-sentences. These are discourse-level mechanisms that recur in architecture documentation regardless of style or component naming.
COREF_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles use follow-up-sentences with definite-anaphoric subjects, and the distinction between action predicates and result predicates is independent of style. Requiring validated antecedent propagation is a general coreference constraint, not a style-specific assumption. Passes.

COREF_RULES.rule_text: Allow anaphora-based propagation only when the antecedent sentence already contains strong element-identification evidence: exact-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, apposition, possessive, namespace-prefix, or section-heading support. Block propagation when the antecedent subject-position is an indefinite or generic multi-word-phrase without such evidence. Anaphora may preserve a validated link, but it may not upgrade a generic antecedent into an element mention.
COREF_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The exact-match element records state. It also reports timing." 
FP: "A lightweight option records state. It also reports timing."
COREF_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule uses only antecedent strength and anaphora licensing conditions. Coreference behavior of this kind is independent of implementation structure because it is governed by discourse reference, not by architecture-specific semantics.
COREF_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in all five, anaphora can validly continue a prior identified mention, but should not inherit from a generic indefinite antecedent. The licensing criterion is purely discourse-based and remains stable across styles. Passes.

COREF_RULES.rule_text: Allow a subject-position pronoun, definite-article phrase, or follow-up-sentence anaphora to inherit a prior link only when the antecedent is explicit and the current sentence supplies compatibility evidence through exact-match, alias-defined-parenthetically, or a matching head-noun plus predicate. Reject nearest-mention propagation when the current predicate frames only destination, surrounding context, comparison, or container-of information rather than identity or function of the antecedent. If multiple antecedents are available, prefer the one whose head-noun and predicate jointly align with the current clause.
COREF_RULES.example_block:
TP: S1: The multi-word-phrase "delta unit" (delta) validates incoming records. S2: It rejects malformed input before follow-up processing.
FP: S1: The namespace-prefix delta appears beside the reporting group in the overview. S2: It sends the summary to the outer interface.
COREF_RULES.why_it_transfers: The rule relies only on antecedent explicitness, subject-position, head-noun compatibility, and predicate compatibility. Those cues are discourse-level and do not depend on any particular decomposition or interaction structure.
COREF_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: in each case, pronouns and definite-article phrases can refer either to the prior element or to nearby context, so antecedent validation by head-noun and predicate remains necessary. The negative cases also remain stable because destination/context predicates do not establish identity in any of the five. Passes.

SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.rule_text: When one mention is asserted by the main predicate and a second mention appears in a purpose qualifier-clause that explicitly sets up separation, contrast, or alias-like correspondence, keep the main-predicate mention as a seed and propagate a second candidate only if the qualifier-clause presents the second mention as a paired counterpart in the same assertion. Do not propagate from a qualifier-clause that states only a generic purpose without a second explicit mention. Prefer asymmetric handling: the main-predicate mention is primary, and the qualifier-clause mention is secondary but still valid when the relation is explicit.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The first element remains distinct from the second element to keep the external phrase separate from the internal phrase." 
FP: "The first element remains distinct to keep the external phrase separate."
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule is based on discourse asymmetry between main assertion and qualifier-clause, plus explicit paired mention structure. It does not assume any specific component type, data concept, or architectural arrangement.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: paired mentions split across main predicate and purpose qualifier-clause can appear in all five, and the distinction between explicit counterpart mention versus generic purpose remains stable. The rule relies only on clause function and mention pairing, not on style-specific terminology. Passes.

SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.rule_text: Treat a reduced form, short form, or namespace-prefix as alias-defined only when local discourse establishes it. Accept alias-of propagation only if an antecedent exact-match appears in a nearby introducing-sentence, apposition, or alias-defined-parenthetically construction; otherwise keep the reduced form ambiguous. A bare head-noun or shortened multi-word-phrase without such establishment must not seed approval.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: An introducing-sentence presents "long phrase (LP)," and a follow-up-sentence uses "LP" with the same antecedent in local context.
FP: A sentence uses only "phrase" after several candidates with similar head-noun forms have appeared, and the linker treats it as alias-of one specific longer candidate without any apposition, parenthetical, or exact-match establishment.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: Alias establishment through antecedent, apposition, and parenthetical introduction is a discourse phenomenon independent of architecture style. The rule constrains abbreviation and reduction using local textual evidence only.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five styles may use shortened references, but the requirement for local antecedent or parenthetical establishment is unchanged across them. The rule uses only discourse cues and avoids any style-bound assumptions. Passes.

SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.rule_text: When the main assertion contains one explicit mention and a trailing qualifier-clause introduces a second explicit mention through a relational predicate of separation, distinction, or decoupling, allow two approved seeds if both mentions are structurally explicit. The second seed must be anchored by its own head-noun mention inside the qualifier-clause, not inferred from an abstract purpose alone. Do not propagate a second seed from a qualifier-clause that contains only a generic benefit statement without an explicit mention.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.example_block:
TP: "The records are placed in the repository element to keep the staging element separate from the index." -> approve the repository element and the staging element as seeds.
FP: "The records are placed in the repository element to improve efficiency." -> do not create a second seed from the qualifier-clause.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.why_it_transfers: This rule relies on explicit mention structure across a main clause and a qualifier-clause, plus a relational predicate that ties two mentions. Such discourse relations are common across documentation styles and do not depend on any specific architecture lexicon.
SEED_DISAMBIGUATION_RULES.abstraction_check_cot: Tested against microservice/event-sourced/layered/pipe-filter/hexagonal: all five can express one mention in the main assertion and another in a purpose qualifier-clause linked by separation or distinction language; the approval criterion is explicit structural anchoring, not style-specific semantics. The guard against generic benefit clauses is equally style-invariant. Passes.
